newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon opposition calls for annulment of poll.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon opposition calls for annulment of poll.

text.p: Cameroon's main opposition has called for annulment of the country's weekend general elections because of alleged massive rigging by the ruling party.

Chief opposition leader John Fru Ndi issued a statement on Sunday calling for the parliamentary elections to be scrapped "in order to save the Cameroonian nation from disaster" and "in the interest of peace in Cameroon."
Officials for his Social Democratic Front (SDF) on Monday denounced claims of a landslide victory by President Paul Biya's Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (RDPC) as a provocation.
The interior ministry which runs elections in Cameroon said it would not issue provisional returns. It has 20 days to announce final results.
However, the cabinet director in the prime minister's office, Pierre Moukoko Mbonjo, told Reuters Biya's party had won between 100 and 110 of the 180 seats in the National Assembly.
The SDF took between 50 and 60 seats and the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP) 10, he said. State radio has broadcast similar provisional results.
An SDF official countered with the party's own claim of victory.
"The chairman (Fru Ndi) told us this morning that we have won at least 97 seats and maybe 110 seats," Genevieve Fouda, an SDF candidate, told Reuters on Monday.

"The radio is only announcing an RDPC victory to provoke us. We call on you to remain calm," she told SDF militants outside the Yaounde party office. "These elections have been rigged on a scale that we have never witnessed before in this republic."
SDF officials whose leader narrowly lost to Biya in a 1992 presidential poll, sounded gloomy on Sunday.
"I am very pessimistic that we will only get 56 seats," Alhaji Sani, its election coordinator, told Reuters.
"The organisation was catastrophic," he said. "Because of rigging we are very pessimistic. So many people did not get cards."

The mood was the same at the Yaounde offices of the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP), which won 68 seats in 1992. "With the fraud we have revised our projection from 35 to 30 seats," said campaign director Pierre Flambeau Ngayap.

The Front, which boycotted Cameroon's 1992 parliamentary election, has its power base in the volatile English-speaking North-West Province but draws support from Cameroon's main ethnic Bamileke group and the urban poor.
North-West Province is a flashpoint in largely French-speaking Cameroon. So far no unrest or violence has been reported.
International observers from three organisations, including the Commonwealth Group of Observers and the French Cultural and Technical Cooperation Agency, declined official comment.
"There are some categories of irregularities," said one observer privately, asking not to be identified.
